own_translation_en: Zayd (Zeid in the text), a companion of Muhammad, had a beautiful wife, and Muhammad desired her. As they were sitting together, Muhammad said: 'Such-and-such, God has ordered me to take your wife.' He answered: 'You are an apostle; do as God told you; take my wife.' Or rather, to put it from the start, he said to him: 'God ordered me that you should divorce your wife.' He divorced her. After many days he said: 'But God ordered that I too should take her.' Then, having taken her and committed adultery with her, he laid down this law: 'Whoever wishes, let him divorce his wife; if after divorcing her he goes back to her, let another marry her...' [the law continues on the brother's marriage, and a note that the rest is too obscene to tell]. (Team translation from the Greek OCR; Latin side is a parallel version.)

Non enim licet eam accipere, nisi ante ductam ab alio : ita ut si frater etiam illam dimiserit, ducatur a fratre ejus, si libuerit. » Porro in scriptura sua ejusmodi quedam pronuntiat : « Operare terram quam tibi dedit Deus, et studiose illam cole : atque hoc facito, et ad hunc modum ; » ne omnia ut ille obscena proferam.

what_it_says: John says that Muhammad coveted his companion Zayd's beautiful wife, obtained her by a claimed divine command, and committed adultery with her, then made a law permitting the marriage.
context: Part of John's refutation of the 'Ishmaelite superstition' in Heresy 101, addressed to a Christian reader against the Qur'an as he knew it (an invented or distorted Qur'anic/Hadith story about Zayd and Zaynab). It is a polemical narrative set among the many 'deliramenta' he attributes to Muhammad; the author writes as an enemy of Islam.
limits: Polemical hostile narrative written 100+ years after the events, about a case that Muslims relate differently (Zayd, Zaynab, the divorce and marriage told in Qur'an 33:37 and in later tradition); the wife is not named, not Aisha, and no age is given. It is about the wife of Zayd, not Muhammad's marriage to a child. Some Greek is OCR-garbled; the Latin is a parallel version and may not be John's own wording. The chapter also depends on Greek OCR from a two-column scan.

own_translation_en: This Muhammad, having composed many nonsense-tales, as has been said, gave a name to each of them. For example, the 'Sura of the Woman': in it he openly legislates that they take four wives, and concubines, if possible a thousand, as many as his hand may hold, apart from the four wives. Whoever wishes to divorce a wife, or wants to, may take another, on such grounds he laid down the law. [...] (Team translation of the Greek OCR; the Latin says 'concubinas, si fieri possit, mille, ... praeter quatuor illas uxores'.)
quote_latin: Mamed ille cum multa deliramenia, ut dictum est, copscripserit, eorum singulis nomina indidit. Cujusmodi est scriptura (Sur. 4), seu caput mulieris, in qua propalam lege sancit quaternas uxorcs accipere, et concubinas, si feri possit, mille, […] quoque manus ejus subditas contineat, prater […] quatuor illas uxores : quam item voluerit, dimittere, aliamque, si allubescat, ducere, ob ejusmodi causam statuit.

what_it_says: John says that Muhammad's law openly allows four wives and as many concubines as possible (he says a thousand), and that Muhammad gave each of his compositions a name (here 'the woman').
context: Same chapter as the Zayd passage; here John summarises the Qur'anic rule on marriage (Sura 4, cited by him) as evidence of Muhammad's lust and of his 'nonsense'. It gives no particular wife and no age.
limits: Describes a legal permission (four wives plus concubines) as the author reads it, not a statement about Aisha or any age. Under the team's rule, the number of wives alone is not a criticism of Aisha's age: this passage is included only as a LUST criticism of Muhammad's sensuality. The Latin says 'quaternas uxores'; the OCR spelling 'παλλαχὰς' is kept as printed; the sura reference 'Sur. 4' is his own citation.
